The gut answer reads the conditional backwards. Ninety-nine percent of sick people test positive. That does NOT mean ninety-nine percent of positives are sick. Bayes' rule turns one into the other, and it can't work without the base rate: how common the disease was before anyone was tested. Healthy people outnumber the sick nearly a thousand to one, so their false alarms beat the real cases ten to one. Forgetting that is base-rate neglect. So test the positives again, with a second, independent test. Ninety-eight of the real cases stay positive... and only about ten of the false alarms. Now nine positives in ten are real. Ninety-one percent. So before you trust a positive, ask how rare the thing is. Conditioning has fooled experts, too.

A game show has three doors. Behind one is a car, and behind the other two, goats. You pick a door. Then the host, who knows where the car is, opens another door... and shows you a goat. Do you switch? In nineteen ninety, a magazine columnist said yes: switching wins two times in three. Thousands of readers wrote in to tell her she was wrong.

She was right. Your first pick hides the car one time in three. The other two times, you've picked a goat... so the host has to open the other goat. The door he leaves shut has the car. His choice isn't random. It depends on where the car is, and that's information. Play a hundred thousand games in code. Staying wins thirty-three percent of them. Switching wins sixty-seven. So far, the outcomes have been labels. Heads, a goat, a positive. To average them, you need numbers.

A random variable puts a number on each outcome. Flip two coins, and count the heads. Two, one, one... or zero.
